entries.question: Does God have a body?
entries.summary: Genesis shows Yahweh strolling through Eden 'in the cool of the day' — audible footsteps, physical movement. John 4:24 and Luke 24:39 then insist God is a spirit who by definition has no flesh and bones. Take your pick: a wandering-through-the-garden deity, or an incorporeal one.
entries.commentary: The apologist move is to call Genesis 3:8 anthropomorphism — God stooping to human language the way a parent uses baby-talk. Gleason Archer runs this play in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, and Walton in his NIVAC Genesis commentary treats the 'walking' as a theophanic accommodation to human limits. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence. But the critical read is more parsimonious: early Israelite Yahwism straightforwardly pictured a corporeal deity, and the later philosophical spirit-God of Hellenistic Judaism and the Johannine community is a theological upgrade, not an original feature. Mark Smith's The Early History of God and Benjamin Sommer's The Bodies of God and the World of Ancient Israel document a robust 'divine body' tradition across the Hebrew Bible — Yahweh eats with Abraham at Mamre, wrestles Jacob, reveals his back to Moses. Sommer's own focus is the Hebrew Bible's divine-body tradition rather than Johannine reception, but his work fits within a broader scholarly picture in which 'God is spirit' looks more like a later philosophical development than an original Israelite axiom. The contradiction is real; the harmonization is an attempt to read later metaphysics back into the earliest strata of the text.

Sommer, Benjamin D. *The Bodies of God and the World of Ancient Israel*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2009 — esp. ch. 1 on the fluidity of divine bodies. Walton, John H. *Genesis*. God is a spirit. John 4:24
				
				  For a spirit hath not flesh and bones. Luke 24:39

commentary_out.commentary:
Genesis 3:8 depicts the humans hearing 'the voice [or sound, Hebrew qol] of YHWH God walking [mithallek] in the garden in the cool of the day.' The hithpael participle mithallek connotes habitual, back-and-forth walking about — the same stem used of Enoch and Noah 'walking with God' (Gen 5:22; 6:9) and of God 'walking' among Israel in the camp (Lev 26:12; Deut 23:14). The plain sense is a deity who moves through space, whose approach is audible. John 4:24 ('God is spirit,' pneuma ho theos) and the risen Jesus' words in Luke 24:39 ('a spirit hath not flesh and bones') articulate, by contrast, an incorporeal conception. The question is whether these represent one coherent doctrine of God or a development across the canon.

The strongest harmonization is the anthropomorphism-as-accommodation argument. Gleason Archer's Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties treats Genesis 3:8 as figurative speech in which the infinite God condescends to finite human language; John Walton's NIV Application Commentary reads the 'walking' as a theophanic accommodation suited to an ancient audience. This argument has a genuine pedigree — Maimonides systematized scriptural anthropomorphism as accommodation in the Guide for the Perplexed, and the rabbinic principle dibra torah kilshon bnei adam ('the Torah speaks in human language') anticipates it. Its weakness is that it is a theological judgment imposed on, rather than derived from, the narrative. Genesis 2-3 (conventionally assigned to the Yahwist) gives no internal signal that the walking is metaphorical; the same material has God forming the human from dust with his hands, planting a garden, breathing into nostrils, and stitching garments of skin. The corporeal portrait is consistent and pervasive, not an isolated figure of speech. To label only the 'walking' a condescension while reading the breathing and the hand-forming as live theology is to apply the accommodation principle selectively, on the basis of a later metaphysics rather than any marker in the text.

A point of philological caution is in order. The phrase here translated 'in the cool of the day' is leruach hayyom — literally 'at the ruach (wind/breath/spirit) of the day.' The traditional rendering 'in the cool of the day' (evening breeze) is well established, but a number of scholars (notably Jeffrey Niehaus) have proposed 'in the wind/storm of the day,' reading the scene as a theophanic approach in a gust rather than a quiet evening stroll. This is one scholarly option, not consensus, and it bears on the tone of the scene more than on the central point: in either rendering the deity is portrayed as approaching bodily and audibly.

Equally important is what the textual evidence does NOT show. It is sometimes claimed that the Septuagint already 'softens' Genesis 3:8 by speaking of 'the sound (phone) of the Lord God walking,' as though the LXX shifted the walking from God to a disembodied sound. But this overstates the data. The Hebrew qol itself already means 'voice/sound,' so the LXX phone is a straightforward, non-interpretive rendering of qol; the Masoretic Text equally reads 'the sound of YHWH God walking.' The grammatical ambiguity — whether the participle 'walking' modifies God or the sound — exists identically in both the Hebrew and the Greek and is not a distinctively Septuagintal accommodation. Whatever softening later interpreters drew from the verse came from exegesis, not from a translational maneuver in the LXX.

The critical read is more parsimonious. Mark Smith's The Early History of God documents that early Israelite Yahwism shared the broadly anthropomorphic theology of its West Semitic milieu, picturing the deity in bodily terms. Benjamin Sommer's The Bodies of God and the World of Ancient Israel goes further, arguing that the Hebrew Bible preserves a 'fluidity' tradition in which God possesses one or more concrete bodies: YHWH eats with Abraham at Mamre (Gen 18), wrestles bodily with Jacob (Gen 32), and shows Moses his 'back' while shielding his 'face' (Exod 33:20-23). Sommer's own focus is the Hebrew Bible's divine-body traditions rather than Johannine reception, but his work situates 'God is spirit' as a later philosophical refinement rather than an original Israelite axiom. The incorporeal God is at home in Hellenistic Jewish thought — Philo of Alexandria allegorizes every anthropomorphism precisely because he holds, on Platonic grounds, that God is asomatos ('bodiless') and that scriptural references to God's hands or feet must be read figuratively. The Fourth Gospel's pneuma theology belongs to that later, philosophically inflected stream, and John 4:24 functions in context as a polemical claim about the nature of true worship ('in spirit and truth') rather than as a primitive Israelite axiom. The harmonization is internally coherent only for a reader already committed to incorporeality; the earliest stratum of the text does not supply it, and the accommodation reading must be retrojected onto narrative material that gives no sign of intending metaphor. Verdict: genuine contradiction reflecting theological development — an embodied early-Israelite Yahweh versus the incorporeal God of Hellenistic-Jewish and Johannine theology.

entries.question: Does God know and see everything?
entries.summary: 1 John 3:20 declares God knows all things. Genesis 3 shows Yahweh wandering the garden asking 'Where art thou?' — an omniscient being doesn't search for the humans he supposedly sees always and everywhere. The contradiction is between a philosophical claim of universal knowledge and a narrative God who has to ask questions.
entries.commentary: Apologists routinely read Genesis 3:9 as a rhetorical or pedagogical question — God isn't actually ignorant of Adam's location; he's giving Adam the chance to confess. Archer runs this line, and Hamilton's NICOT Genesis makes a similar move. Fair enough as a pastoral reading, but the text itself shows no such signal. Walton's Lost World of Genesis One pushes a cognitive-environment approach where Genesis portrays God in anthropomorphic terms because that is how ancient Near Eastern audiences encountered deities. That concession is the honest one — and it's the critical position: the Yahwist (J) source pictures a limited deity who walks, asks, changes his mind, and reacts to events. The systematic theology of omniscience is a much later development, crystallized through Hellenistic Jewish writers like Philo and later Christian scholastics. James Kugel in How to Read the Bible calls this the 'small God' of early Israel — a deity with real cognitive limits whose personality the redactors never fully scrubbed out. The apologist harmonization requires importing centuries of philosophical theology into a text that doesn't supply it.
entries.scholarship: Kugel, James L. *How to Read the Bible: A Guide to Scripture, Then and Now*. New York: Free Press, 2007 — ch. on the God of Old. Sommer, Benjamin D. *The Bodies of God and the World of Ancient Israel*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2009. Walton, John H. *The Lost World of Genesis One*. Downers Grove: IVP Academic, 2009. Hamilton, Victor P. *The Book of Genesis, Chapters 1-17*. NICOT. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1990 — commentary on Gen 3:8-9. Archer, Gleason L. *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties*. Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 1982.

answers.answer: God sees and knows all things.
There are some things that God doesn't know and can't see.
answers.answer_explanation: And Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the Lord, amongst the trees of the garden. And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou? Genesis 3:8-9

commentary_out.commentary:
1 John 3:20 asserts that God 'knoweth all things' (ginōskei panta) — a compact statement of divine omniscience consonant with later systematic theology. Genesis 3:8-9 narrates a scene that, read flatly, points the other way: God 'walking in the garden,' the humans hiding among the trees, and God calling out 'Where art thou?' (Hebrew ayyekkah). On its face an all-knowing deity does not search for hidden creatures or pose locational questions. The issue is whether the question signals genuine ignorance or functions as something else.

The strongest harmonization treats the question as rhetorical or pedagogical rather than informational, and it is more strongly grounded in the narrative than critics sometimes allow. Archer's Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties and Victor Hamilton's NICOT commentary argue that God knows perfectly well where Adam is; the question is an invitation to confession, a summons granting the human the dignity of self-disclosure — much as a parent who has already seen the broken vase asks 'What happened here?' Crucially, this reading is not a bare imposition: the narrative itself supplies the confession dynamic. Genesis 3:10-13 unfolds precisely as an elicitation of admission — 'Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree...?' — followed by the man's deflection onto the woman and the woman's onto the serpent. The interrogative sequence reads naturally as a forensic inquest in which the questioner draws out testimony, not as a search by a baffled deity. This is a long-standing reading: Augustine and the rabbinic tradition both took ayyekkah as a merciful overture rather than a literal request for coordinates.

The related divine 'investigation' texts are similarly susceptible to a forensic-idiom reading. Genesis 18:21 ('I will go down now, and see... and if not, I will know') uses descent-and-inspection language that many interpreters, including conservatives, read as judicial idiom — the formal establishment of a legal case before sentence — rather than literal acquisition of unknown facts, comparable to a judge's 'taking cognizance.' On this view Genesis 4:9 ('Where is Abel thy brother?') and 11:5 ('the LORD came down to see the city') belong to the same rhetorical register of judicial summons and condescending narrative. This is a mainstream, internally defensible option, and it considerably softens the tension.

What keeps the matter from full resolution is that the Yahwist's portrait does not stop at courtroom idiom. The same narrative stream shows God 'repenting' (nacham) that he made humanity (Gen 6:6), being grieved at heart, and reacting to events as they unfold — a deity drawn in genuinely interactive, temporally engaged terms. Mark Smith's and Benjamin Sommer's work situates this within an early Israelite theology in which YHWH is locally present and embodied rather than abstractly omniscient. John Walton's cognitive-environment approach (The Lost World of Genesis One) concedes that Genesis depicts God in the anthropomorphic terms through which ancient Near Eastern audiences encountered deities. James Kugel's How to Read the Bible describes the comparatively limited God of Old — a figure perceived in local, bodily terms whose personality the later editors never fully smoothed away. The doctrine of exhaustive omniscience is a later crystallization: Hellenistic Jewish writers, Philo above all, fused the biblical God with the all-knowing mind of Greek philosophy, and Christian scholastics systematized it; 1 John, written within that developed milieu, states the principle flatly.

The honest assessment, then, is two-layered. At the level of Genesis 3 read on its own terms, the rhetorical/judicial-question reading is a legitimate, text-grounded harmonization — the confession sequence in vv. 10-13 is real internal evidence, not imported metaphysics. But across the wider J narrative the deity is portrayed with cognitive and spatial limits that a thoroughgoing omniscience does not easily absorb, and that broader portrait reflects a genuinely earlier conception of God than 1 John's. Verdict: partially harmonized — the specific 'Where art thou?' resolves plausibly as a confession-eliciting summons, but it sits within an early-Israelite portrait of a limited, reactive God that stands in real tension with later omniscience doctrine.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Within Genesis 3 itself the question 'Where art thou?' can be read as a rhetorical, confession-eliciting summons rather than a request for information: vv.10-13 unfold as a forensic inquest drawing out admission, and the parallel 'investigation' texts (Gen 18:21, 'that I may know') are widely read as judicial idiom for establishing a case rather than literal ignorance. This is a mainstream, internally grounded reading. The residual tension is that the wider Yahwist portrait (God 'repenting,' reacting, locally present) reflects an earlier, limited conception of deity that later omniscience doctrine (1 John 3:20, crystallized via Philo and the scholastics) does not fully absorb.

entries.question: Does God desire animal sacrifices?
entries.summary: The Priestly source and the Genesis narrative have Yahweh approving Abel's animal sacrifice and later filling Leviticus with hundreds of verses of mandatory blood offerings. Psalms 40, 50, and 51 then say God does not desire sacrifice or burnt offerings at all. The cult system the Torah makes compulsory is what the Psalter, and later the prophets, dismiss as unwanted.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization is that the Psalms and prophets are not rejecting sacrifice as such — they're rejecting sacrifice without contrition. Derek Kidner's Tyndale commentary on Psalms and Tremper Longman both argue for a 'relative negation' reading: what God really wants is obedience and a broken heart, not mechanical ritual. That is a standard rabbinic and Christian reading and it has textual support — Psalm 51 does pair the rejection with a call for a contrite heart. But the critical read pushes harder. Jacob Milgrom's monumental Anchor Bible Leviticus volumes and Jonathan Klawans in Purity, Sacrifice, and the Temple argue that these passages reflect a real internal dispute in ancient Israel between temple-cult insiders and prophetic/sapiential critics — an actual historical conflict between the P/H priestly tradition and a non-cultic piety stream visible in certain Psalms and in prophets like Amos and Hosea. Put bluntly: the Bible preserves competing schools on whether Yahweh wanted the slaughter at all. The harmonization flattens what is actually a polyphonic argument inside the text. Take your pick — but you cannot read all of these verses as one coherent voice.
entries.scholarship: Milgrom, Jacob. *Leviticus 1-16*. Anchor Bible 3. New York: Doubleday, 1991 — introduction on the sacrificial system. Klawans, Jonathan. *Purity, Sacrifice, and the Temple: Symbolism and Supersessionism in the Study of Ancient Judaism*. New York: Oxford University Press, 2006 — ch. on prophetic critique of sacrifice. Heschel, Abraham J. *The Prophets*. New York: Harper & Row, 1962. Kidner, Derek. *Psalms 1-72*. Tyndale OT Commentary. Downers Grove: IVP, 1973 — commentary on Pss 40, 50, 51. Anderson, Gary A. *Sacrifices and Offerings in Ancient Israel*. HSM 41. Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1987.

answers.answer: No, God does not desire animal sacrifices.
answers.answer_explanation:
Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire. Psalm 40:6
				    
				    Will I eat of the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of
				          goats? Psalm 50:13
				    
				    
For thou desirest not sacrifice ... thou delightest not in
				          burnt offerings. Psalm 51:16

commentary_out.commentary:
Genesis 4:4 reports YHWH's regard for Abel's animal offering, and the Priestly legislation of Leviticus makes blood sacrifice the mandatory center of Israelite worship. Yet Psalm 40:6 ('sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire'), Psalm 50:13 ('Will I eat the flesh of bulls?'), and Psalm 51:16 ('thou desirest not sacrifice... thou delightest not in burnt offerings') appear to repudiate the very cult the Torah commands. The same posture recurs in the prophets — Amos 5:21-24, Hosea 6:6 ('I desired mercy, and not sacrifice'), Isaiah 1:11-17, Jeremiah 7:21-23, Micah 6:6-8.

The traditional harmonization reads these as instances of 'relative' or 'dialectical' negation, a recognized Hebrew idiom in which a stark 'not X but Y' actually means 'Y more than X.' Derek Kidner's Tyndale Psalms commentary and Tremper Longman argue that the Psalms and prophets reject sacrifice offered hypocritically, without obedience or a contrite heart — not the institution itself. The internal evidence is genuinely strong. Psalm 51 pairs the rejection of sacrifice (v. 16) with the claim that 'the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit' (v. 17), and then, in vv. 18-19, anticipates that God will 'be pleased with the sacrifices of righteousness, with burnt offering and whole burnt offering' once Zion is rebuilt — the psalm as we have it ends affirming the cult, not abolishing it. Hosea 6:6 uses the comparative construction (mercy 'and not' sacrifice) that Jesus later cites approvingly (Matt 9:13; 12:7) without any sense of abolishing the Temple. On this reading the texts critique misuse, not use. The idiom is well documented elsewhere: Proverbs 8:10 ('receive my instruction, and not silver') does not forbid silver, and the 'not... but' of comparative Hebrew rhetoric is a standard way of expressing priority rather than negation.

A critical caveat sharpens the picture rather than dissolving it. Psalm 51:18-19 is widely regarded by critical scholars and noted in many commentaries as a likely post-exilic editorial appendix: vv. 16-17 reject sacrifice outright, and vv. 18-19 — invoking the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls — reverse course to affirm restored-Temple offerings. The most economical explanation is that a later editor added the closing couplet precisely to reconcile the psalm's anti-sacrifice statement with re-established cultic worship; the shift from individual penitence to corporate restoration, and the explicit reference to walls not yet standing, are the standard internal grounds. This cuts two ways. At the canonical level it supports the harmonization, since the received text does end by endorsing sacrifice. But it also illustrates, in microcosm, the very editorial reconciliation of competing stances that the critical reading posits — the tension was real enough that someone felt obliged to resolve it within the text itself.

The history behind these passages is contested. Jacob Milgrom's Anchor Bible Leviticus situates the offerings within a coherent priestly system in which sacrifice is not magic but a structured response to sin and impurity. Jonathan Klawans's Purity, Sacrifice, and the Temple is important here precisely because Klawans argues AGAINST the older supersessionist reading that pitted 'spiritual' prophets against a 'mechanical' cult: he contends the prophets did not reject sacrifice per se but condemned its misuse, and he is therefore better cited on the harmonizing, relative-negation side than as evidence of a cult-versus-anti-cult historical war. Abraham Heschel's The Prophets frames the prophetic protest as directed against a cult divorced from justice — worship that proceeds while the poor are crushed — again a critique of misuse rather than of the institution. Gary Anderson's study of Israelite sacrifice situates the offerings within a broader economy of gift and divine pleasure that the prophets could invoke critically without repudiating. Where genuine scholarly disagreement remains is over the sharpest formulations — Jeremiah 7:22, 'I spake not unto your fathers... concerning burnt offerings,' which on its face denies that sacrifice was part of the original Sinai mandate at all, and the bluntest Amos and Isaiah oracles — which some read as hyperbole within the relative-negation idiom and others as evidence of a real diversity of evaluative stances toward the cult preserved side by side in the canon. Jeremiah 7:22 is especially hard to fold cleanly into comparative negation, since it makes a historical claim about what was commanded, not merely a ranking of priorities.

The upshot: the relative-negation reading is well grounded and resolves most of the surface contradiction. The Psalms, on balance, subordinate sacrifice to obedience and contrition rather than abolishing it, and Psalm 51 as transmitted closes by affirming the cult — even if that closing is itself an editorial harmonization. Beneath the idiom, however, the canon plainly preserves more than one emphasis, and the sharpest prophetic lines are not fully tamed by the comparative reading. The Genesis 4 and Leviticus material reflects a priestly piety in which sacrifice is central and divinely desired; certain Psalms and prophetic oracles reflect a sapiential and prophetic piety in which it is, at best, secondary. Verdict: largely harmonizable via relative negation (critique of cult-without-obedience), with a residual, deliberately transmitted diversity of emphasis between priestly and prophetic-sapiential pieties.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The Psalm texts read most naturally as rhetorical/comparative negation ('I desire obedience rather than ritual'), rejecting sacrifice offered without contrition rather than sacrifice as such — Ps 51 pairs the rejection with a plea for a broken heart and ends (vv.18-19) affirming acceptable offerings. This is the rabbinic and traditional reading; Klawans's work argues the prophets likewise critiqued misuse rather than the cult itself. The residual tension is genuine: Ps 51:18-19 is widely judged a post-exilic editorial appendix reconciling the psalm, and the sharpest prophetic formulations (Jer 7:22; Amos 5:21-24) reflect a diversity of evaluative stances preserved in the canon.

entries.question: Is polygamy OK?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, 1 Timothy, Titus
entries.summary: This one is a three-way tangle. The Hebrew Bible narrates polygamy without condemnation across patriarchs, judges, and kings — Abraham, Jacob, Gideon, David, Solomon, Rehoboam all pile up wives. Genesis 2:24 frames marriage as one man and one woman becoming one flesh. The Pastoral Epistles then restrict monogamy specifically to bishops, implying laypeople can still have multiple wives.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization runs through dispensationalism and ideal-versus-permitted categories: Genesis 2 states the creation ideal, the patriarchal and monarchic polygamy is narrative description under divine tolerance (not endorsement), and the Pastorals tighten things for church leaders. Blomberg and Köstenberger both run versions of this. That scaffolding is doing enormous work to reconcile a corpus that never once condemns polygamy outright. The critical read is more direct. Deuteronomy 21:15-17 regulates polygamy rather than prohibits it. David Instone-Brewer in Marriage and Divorce in the Bible and the Ancient Near East documents that Second Temple Jewish sources show polygamy remained legal and practiced among Jews into the first century. The Pastoral Epistles' 'husband of one wife' (mias gunaikos andra) phrase is disputed — it may mean 'faithful to one wife,' 'married only once' (prohibiting remarriage after divorce or widowhood), or literally 'monogamous.' Luke Timothy Johnson's Anchor Bible commentary on the Pastorals walks through all three readings without endorsing one. Meanwhile Genesis 2:24 describes the creation-week pairing, not a universal marriage law. So the Bible's actual position on polygamy is: tolerated, never commanded, never explicitly banned, and later ecclesiastical limits applied only to leadership. Modern Christian monogamy is a post-biblical norm read back into the text.
entries.scholarship: Instone-Brewer, David. *Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible: The Social and Literary Context*. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 2002 — chs. on Second Temple practice. commentary_out.commentary:
The question braids three threads. First, the Hebrew Bible narrates polygamy across patriarchs (Abraham via Hagar, Jacob with Leah, Rachel, and their maids, Esau), judges (Gideon, who 'had many wives,' Judg 8:30), and kings (David, Solomon's seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, Rehoboam's eighteen wives, Abijah's fourteen) without any explicit condemnation of the plurality as such, and the Torah legislates for it rather than against it. Second, Genesis 2:24 frames the primal pairing as one man and one woman becoming 'one flesh.' Third, the Pastoral Epistles require that a bishop be 'the husband of one wife' (1 Tim 3:2; Titus 1:6), a restriction whose specificity to office-holders implies it was not a universal rule.

The apologetic harmonization runs through the categories of creation-ideal versus tolerated-deviation, often with a dispensational inflection, and it is more substantial than a bare appeal to Genesis 2. The case has three legs: (1) Genesis 2:24 states a monogamous creation ideal — 'they shall be one flesh,' singular; (2) the plural marriages of the patriarchs and kings are narrated descriptively under divine forbearance and are consistently shadowed by strife, which functions as implicit authorial disapproval (the Sarah-Hagar conflict, Jacob's rival wives, Solomon's foreign wives turning his heart in 1 Kgs 11, Deut 17:17's warning that the king not 'multiply wives'); and (3) Jesus appeals to Genesis 2:24 (Matt 19:4-6; Mark 10:6-8) to ground an exclusive, indissoluble union, exhibiting an inner-biblical trajectory back toward the creation pattern. Köstenberger and Jones develop this in God, Marriage, and Family, and Craig Blomberg argues along similar lines. Importantly, these defenders do not claim the Old Testament contains an explicit prohibition of polygamy; they claim a normative ideal plus a tolerated, problematized deviation that the canon progressively narrows.

The critical analysis grants the trajectory but resists the conclusion that the corpus speaks with one normative voice. The Torah does not merely tolerate polygamy; it actively regulates it. Exodus 21:10 protects the conjugal rights of a first wife when a man takes a second; Deuteronomy 21:15-17 governs inheritance 'if a man have two wives, one beloved, and another hated' — legislation that presupposes and accommodates the practice rather than discouraging it. The royal law of Deuteronomy 17:17 cautions only against multiplying wives to excess, not against having more than one. Michael Satlow's Jewish Marriage in Antiquity and David Instone-Brewer document that polygamy remained legally permissible and occasionally practiced among Jews into the Roman period; it was not formally renounced in Ashkenazi Judaism until the medieval ban (herem) attributed to Rabbenu Gershom around 1000 CE. Against this background, Genesis 2:24 reads most naturally as an etiology — explaining why a man leaves his parents and cleaves to a wife — rather than as a marriage statute, and it says nothing explicit about plural marriage.

The Pastorals' phrase mias gunaikos andra ('a one-woman man') is genuinely disputed. Luke Timothy Johnson's Anchor Bible commentary lays out three live readings without forcing one: (a) literally monogamous, excluding polygamists; (b) 'faithful to his one wife,' i.e., marital fidelity; or (c) 'married only once,' prohibiting remarriage after widowhood or divorce — a reading favored by much patristic interpretation and paralleled by the requirement for enrolled widows in 1 Tim 5:9 ('the wife of one man'). On readings (b) and (c) the verse is not about polygamy at all. Even on reading (a), attaching the restriction specifically to overseers and deacons implies monogamy was not simply assumed of every believer, or the qualification would be redundant.

Where does this leave the dispute? The apologists are right that no biblical text commands polygamy and that an inner-biblical trajectory toward exclusive, lifelong union is real, climaxing in Jesus' citation of Genesis 2. The critics are right that no text bans it either, that the Law accommodates and regulates it, that Second Temple Judaism still permitted it, and that the Pastoral restriction is both office-specific and lexically contested. The genuine point of disagreement is therefore not whether an explicit prohibition exists (it does not, and serious defenders do not claim one) but whether descriptive tolerance plus an idealized trajectory amounts to a binding monogamous norm. That is a question of interpretive weighting on which the evidence underdetermines the answer. Verdict: disputed — Scripture tolerates and regulates polygamy and never bans it, while also displaying a creation-ideal and a narrowing trajectory toward monogamy; whether that trajectory constitutes a normative rule is a real interpretive divide, not a simple contradiction or a clean harmonization.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The apologetic case is a creation-ideal-with-tolerated-deviation trajectory, not a claim of explicit prohibition: Gen 2:24 (singular 'one flesh'), the consistent narrative association of polygamy with strife, and Jesus' citation of Gen 2:24 (Matt 19; Mark 10) trace an inner-biblical movement toward exclusive union. The countervailing data are equally real: the Torah regulates rather than forbids polygamy (Exod 21:10; Deut 21:15-17), Second Temple Judaism still permitted it, and the Pastorals' 'one-woman man' is office-specific and lexically ambiguous (Johnson's three readings). The dispute is whether tolerance plus an idealized trajectory amounts to a normative monogamous rule — an interpretive divide the evidence underdetermines.

entries.question: Was Enoch the sixth or the seventh from Adam?
entries.summary: Count Adam as position one and the Genesis 5 genealogy puts Enoch at position seven. Count Adam as position zero and he's the sixth. Jude 14 says 'Enoch, the seventh from Adam' and the SAB parenthetical note is correct: Jude is quoting 1 Enoch 60:8, not Genesis. The contradiction is really about where your counting starts.
entries.commentary: This one should probably get flagged for human review because it hinges on whether inclusive counting is considered a contradiction at all. The ancient convention, and the one Jude uses, is inclusive counting: Adam is position one, Enoch is position seven. Genesis 5:3-18 lists Adam → Seth → Enos → Cainan → Mahalaleel → Jared → Enoch, which is seven names inclusive and six generations. Luke 3:37-38 and 1 Chronicles 1:1-2 just list the names; they don't specify a count, so the SAB's 'sixth from Adam' framing is an inference by the author, not a claim made by Luke or Chronicles themselves. Richard Bauckham's Jude, 2 Peter commentary in the Word Biblical Commentary and James VanderKam's extensive work on the Enochic literature both note that 'seventh from Adam' is a stock epithet in Second Temple Jewish sources (1 Enoch 60:8, 93:3; Jubilees 7:39) and carries significance — the seventh generation is a position of sabbatical completion and cosmic authority in apocalyptic literature. So Jude is invoking an established Enochic tradition, not miscounting Genesis. The contradiction as stated is weak — it's really a dispute about counting convention. Recommend the SAB rewrite this one around Jude's use of 1 Enoch as scripture, which is a much stronger contradiction (canonical issues).

commentary_out.commentary:
The alleged contradiction is whether Enoch was the sixth or the seventh generation from Adam. Genesis 5:3-18 traces Adam → Seth → Enosh → Cainan (Kenan) → Mahalalel → Jared → Enoch. Counted inclusively, with Adam as position one, Enoch stands at position seven; counted as generations after Adam, he is the sixth. Jude 14 calls him 'Enoch, the seventh from Adam.' The 1 Chronicles 1:1-2 and Luke 3:37-38 parallels merely list the names in order; neither assigns Enoch a numeral. The 'sixth from Adam' framing is therefore the questioner's inference (reckoning generations after Adam), not an assertion any biblical text makes.

The resolution is a matter of counting convention, and it favors Jude straightforwardly. Inclusive counting — where the starting point is itself counted as 'one' — is the normal ancient idiom (the same convention that makes the resurrection 'on the third day' rather than 'after two days'). On inclusive reckoning the seven names of Genesis 5 yield Enoch as the seventh, exactly as Jude says. There is no arithmetical conflict; the two figures simply reflect inclusive versus exclusive counting of one and the same list. The genealogies in Chronicles and Luke neither support nor undercut Jude — they supply the identical sequence of names and decline to number it.

More importantly, 'seventh from Adam' is not Jude doing arithmetic on Genesis at all; it is a fixed epithet drawn from the Enochic literature. A point of precision matters here, since the SAB's parenthetical note and the inherited summary have repeated an error: Jude 14-15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 — 'Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, to execute judgment upon all' — nearly verbatim. It does NOT quote 1 Enoch 60:8. Rather, the designation 'seventh from Adam' is a separate, traditional title for Enoch that circulated across the Enochic corpus. It is reflected in the Parables/Similitudes at 1 Enoch 60:8, which refers to Enoch as taken up, 'the seventh from Adam,' and the cognate generational formulation appears in the Apocalypse of Weeks at 1 Enoch 93:3, where Enoch declares he was 'born the seventh in the first week.' The precise textual locus of the fixed epithet is debated and is best cited cautiously rather than pinned decisively to a single verse; what is secure is that 'seventh' is a stock Enochic honorific carrying sabbatical significance, not a number Jude computed from Genesis. Jude has woven together the prophetic quotation from 1 Enoch 1:9 and the traditional honorific 'seventh from Adam' that circulated independently in the Enochic tradition. Conflating the quoted text (1 Enoch 1:9) with the epithet — as the SAB note does in citing '1 Enoch 60:8' as the source of Jude's quotation — is precisely the slip that should not be carried forward.

Richard Bauckham's Word Biblical Commentary on Jude and James VanderKam's studies of the Enochic corpus note that the number seven is significant rather than incidental: the seventh generation marks a position of sabbatical completion and special sanctity in apocalyptic thought, fitting for the figure who 'walked with God' and was translated to heaven (Gen 5:24). George Nickelsburg's Hermeneia commentary on 1 Enoch likewise treats 'seventh from Adam' as a traditional title underscoring Enoch's privileged, sabbatical status, and identifies Jude's quotation as drawn from 1 Enoch 1:9. The Jubilees tradition also celebrates Enoch as a primordial scribe and witness, but it does not employ the exact 'seventh from Adam' phrase, so appeals to Jubilees for that specific epithet should be checked against the standard editions rather than assumed. In any case, Jude is invoking an established tradition, and his number harmonizes with the Genesis list under the standard inclusive convention.

Given all this, the contradiction as posed is weak: it dissolves into a difference of counting convention and a traditional epithet, with neither Luke nor Chronicles actually asserting a competing number. The genuinely substantive issue lurking in the entry is the one the SAB itself flags parenthetically — that Jude treats 1 Enoch, a book outside the Hebrew and Protestant canons, as authoritative prophecy ('Enoch... prophesied,' Jude 14), quoting it as Scripture. That raises real questions about canon and about the New Testament's use of pseudepigrapha, and it would make a far sharper entry than the counting puzzle. Verdict: harmonized — the 'discrepancy' is an inclusive-versus-exclusive counting artifact, and 'seventh from Adam' is a traditional Enochic epithet (reflected in the Enochic corpus, e.g. 1 Enoch 60:8 and the cognate 'seventh in the first week' at 93:3) fully consistent with the Genesis genealogy; the stronger contradiction here is canonical, not numerical.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The discrepancy is an artifact of counting convention. Genesis 5:3-18 lists Adam, Seth, Enosh, Cainan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch — seven names by inclusive reckoning (Adam counted as one), the standard ancient convention Jude follows. 1 Chronicles 1:1-2 and Luke 3:37-38 list only names and assert no number; 'sixth from Adam' is the questioner's own exclusive count, not a claim of those texts. Jude 14's 'seventh from Adam' is moreover a traditional Enochic epithet reflected across the corpus (1 Enoch 60:8; cf. the cognate 'seventh in the first week' at 93:3), whose precise locus is debated and best cited cautiously. (Note: Jude 14-15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, not 60:8.)

issues.problem: The commentary asserts that the exact phrase 'seventh from Adam' is 'most clearly attested at 1 Enoch 60:8, in the Parables/Similitudes, which explicitly speaks of "the seventh from Adam."' This is incorrect. 1 Enoch 60:8 does not contain the phrase 'seventh from Adam'; the verse refers to 'my grandfather was taken up, the seventh from Adam' in some renderings — but the standard scholarly view is that the precise epithet 'seventh from Adam' as a fixed title is not located at 60:8 in the way claimed, and Jude's epithet is generally regarded as drawn from the broader Enochic 'seventh' tradition (e.g., 1 Enoch 93:3, the Apocalypse of Weeks). The commentary builds an elaborate distinction (60:8 = exact epithet vs 93:3 = cognate motif) on a citation that is not securely verifiable as the locus of the exact phrase.
issues.correction: Do not present 1 Enoch 60:8 as the secure, explicit source of the exact phrase 'seventh from Adam.' State accurately that 'seventh from Adam' is a traditional Enochic designation reflected in the Enochic corpus (with 1 Enoch 93:3 'born the seventh in the first week' as the clearest generational basis), and that 60:8 contains a reference to Enoch as taken up but the precise epithet's textual locus should be cited cautiously.
